paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, biographers of eighteenth-century writers mined their subjects' correspondence as though it offered unmediated access to private feeling, the place where the public mask finally slipped. Recent scholarship has made that confidence harder to sustain. Letters of the period were seldom private in our sense: they were routinely read aloud to assembled households, copied into commonplace books, and passed among acquaintances, and their writers, well aware of this circulation, composed them with an eye to audiences beyond the nominal recipient. Manuals of epistolary style, which sold briskly, taught readers how to sound spontaneous, a skill that presupposes that spontaneity was something to be achieved rather than simply expressed. None of this renders the letters worthless to the biographer. It does, however, alter what they can be taken to show. A letter that professes grief may tell us less about the intensity of its writer's sorrow than about the conventions by which sorrow was expected to be displayed, and that, perhaps, is the more recoverable truth.
